units.translation: [Ag. 1268 ἀγαθώ [good] corrupt from ἐγώ [I].] Since the comparative αγαθώτερος [better] and superlative άγαθώτατος [best] are foreign to the usage of the ancient Attic writers, these degrees are supplied from other adjectives, which we will treat each in its own place, insofar as they are found in Aeschylus: ἀμείνων ἀρείων βέλτερος βελτίων κρείσσων λῴων [better], ἄριστος βέλτατος βέλτιστος κράτιστος λῷστος [best].
A prudent, just, good, pious man.
Wise and good men as fellow-rowers.
Of a great and good life that orders the city.
May the good intention of good men be for the citizens.
Good prayers, requitals of good things.
But may you abound with good things in return for good.
May the good things be brought to fulfillment.
better, better, better, better, stronger, better; best, best, best, strongest, best
without milk, not nourished with milk
lacking milk, not nourished with milk

The forms from the nominative ἀγάλαξ [without milk] are more frequent in the oblique cases, so that here too ἀγάλακτα [without milk] might seem to be written with Wecklein in Rheinisches Museum vol. 26 p. 149, which accurately corresponds to the short final syllable of the antistrophic verse 727 ἀπέδειξεν [he showed], although not necessarily, since in this kind of meter there is room for an anceps syllable. Moreover, the common description of the verses of this strophe is correct, which is confirmed by the words ending in the same places in strophe and antistrophe, and it should not be changed in the way Wecklein proposed.
But a herdsman reared him in his house, a lion cub without milk, loving the breast.
it is everything in which one takes delight, as the grammarians interpret it, an ornament, a glory
Horses, the pride of his excessive luxury.
Child, the glory of the house.
And the unshaken glory of wealth.
The altar-protecting glory of the Greek gods.
Suppliant branches, the images of revered Zeus.
Do you again utter words while touching the images?
To the images of the gods.
everything in which one takes delight
Ἀγαμέμνων [Agamemnon] is the title of the surviving tragedy of Aeschylus

Thus I have emended what is absurdly interpolated in M: ἐμοὶ δ᾽ ὅτι μὲν ὁμαλὸς ὁ γάμος | ἄφοβος οὐ δέδια [but as for me, that marriage is even, I do not fear it], about which I spoke in the Preface to the London edition of Prometheus, 1866, p. XV.
But for me, my life is still even and unmarried in my father's house.
but as for me, that marriage is even, I do not fear it
which the glossators explain by λίαν [excessively].
